scenes.say: Throw an exception in the middle of a function, and your cleanup line never runs. By the end, you'll write C plus plus that can't leak, even when exceptions fly, and pick the right smart pointer in one sentence.

lines.text: Pick the pointer in one sentence.

scenes.say: Today you will do three things. Tie cleanup to a destructor, so exceptions cannot skip it. Pick between unique, shared and weak pointers. And break the cycle that leaks even smart pointers.
lines: RAII: acquire in constructor, free in destructor
Break the cycle that leaks shared_ptr

scenes.title: Close the file, even on a throw
scenes.statement: A function opens a file, then something throws. The close call after the throw never runs.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. A function opens a file, then something throws. The close call below it never runs. We want the file closed anyway.

scenes.head: A self-closing door
scenes.say: Think of a self closing door. Walking in opens it. However you leave, it closes behind you. The constructor is the opening. The destructor is the closing, and it always runs.

scenes.head: The bug: close is skipped
scenes.say: Here is the bug. We open a file, print open, then throw. The close call is never reached, and main just catches. The output shows open, then caught. Nothing closed the file.

panels.label: bug

scenes.head: The fix: a File class
scenes.say: The fix is a class. The constructor opens the file. The destructor closes it. Copying is deleted, so two objects never close one file. Now work just makes a File and throws. Open, then close, then caught.

setup.t.cpp:
#include "file.cpp"
int main() { try { work(); } catch (int) { puts("caught"); } }

scenes.say: Your turn. Three Files, a, b and c, are built in that order. Then a throw. Which one closes first? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Files a, b, c built in that order, then a throw. Which closes first?

scenes.head: Unwinding: reverse order
scenes.say: c closes first. Work builds a, b and c in that order, then throws. The stack unwinds, and every finished local is destroyed in reverse: c, then b, then a. No try, no catch, no cleanup code. One fine print: if nothing catches the exception, unwinding is not guaranteed.

scenes.head: RAII is everywhere
scenes.say: You already use it. Heap memory: unique pointer, vector, string. Files: fstream. Locks: lock guard. Threads: j thread joins for you, in C plus plus twenty.

scenes.title: Own a Widget, never delete it
scenes.statement: Make a Widget on the heap with no delete to forget, no leak and no double free. Then hand it to someone else.
scenes.say: Picture this. We need a Widget on the heap. No delete to forget, no leak, no double free. And we can hand it to someone else.

scenes.head: Keys to a room
scenes.say: Think of keys to a room. A unique pointer is the only key. Hand it over, never copy it. A shared pointer is many keys, and the last one out turns off the light. A weak pointer is a note with the room number, no key.

scenes.head: unique_ptr: one owner
scenes.say: Make unique builds a Widget owned by p. You cannot copy a unique pointer: that line would not compile, since two owners would both delete it. You can move it. Now p is null, and r owns the Widget. At the end, r deletes it once.
Quick one. A raw pointer is eight bytes on this machine. How big are a unique pointer and a shared pointer? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: The price of sharing
scenes.say: Eight and sixteen. A unique pointer is a raw pointer's size, so no extra cost. A shared pointer carries two pointers: one to the object, one to a control block, the shared counter beside it. Use unique by default.

scenes.title: When does the Widget die?
scenes.statement: Several owners share one object. Delete it exactly once, when the last owner lets go.

example.input: a, b = a, b dies, a.reset()

scenes.say: Three owners share one object. Who deletes it, and when? Exactly once, when the last owner lets go.

scenes.head: The last one out
scenes.say: Think of people in a room with the lights on. Each person who enters adds one. Each person who leaves subtracts one. The last one out turns off the lights, and that is the delete.

scenes.head: Watch the count
scenes.say: make shared builds the int and a counter, starting at one. Copying a into b adds one: two. When the block ends, b dies and the count drops to one. Then reset releases the last owner. The count hits zero, and the int is deleted.

scenes.head: use_count in code
scenes.say: Same thing in code. One owner prints one. Inside the block, b joins, and it prints two. After the block, back to one. After reset, a is empty, and the count prints zero.
Twist time. Now b takes a by move, not by copy. What does b's use count print? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Move adds no owner
scenes.say: One. A move transfers ownership, so nobody is added, and a becomes empty. A copy adds an owner. A move does not.

scenes.head: Counting is not free
scenes.say: Counting costs something. A copy updates the count in one indivisible step, called atomic. Safe across threads, but slower than a plain add. So do not pass shared pointers by value unless the function keeps one. Pass a reference, or better, the object. The counter is thread safe. The Widget is not.

scenes.title: Two nodes that own each other
scenes.statement: A Parent owns its Child with a shared_ptr. The Child holds a shared_ptr back. Both variables go out of scope.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. A Parent owns its Child with a shared pointer. The Child holds a shared pointer back to its Parent. Both go out of scope. Are they freed?

scenes.head: Neither hangs up first
scenes.say: Think of two people on the phone, each waiting for the other to hang up first. Nobody ever does. Parent and Child are the callers. Each keeps the other alive.

scenes.head: The cycle, with counts
scenes.say: p makes a Parent, count one. The Parent makes a Child, count one. The Child points back, so the Parent's count is two. Now p dies. The Parent drops to one, not zero. Each keeps the other alive, so no destructor ever runs.

scenes.head: No message: a leak
scenes.say: Here is main. The counts are two and one. The scope ends, and nothing prints. No tilde Parent, no tilde Child. A leak, though we never wrote new.
Try this one. The Child's back link becomes a weak pointer. When p dies, what happens? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: The fix: a weak back link
scenes.say: Decide who owns whom. The Parent owns its Child with a shared pointer. The Child only observes, with a weak pointer that adds nothing to the count. When p dies, the Parent's count hits zero, its destructor runs, and its members go too. Both messages print.

scenes.head: Using a weak_ptr: lock it
scenes.say: A weak pointer cannot be used directly. Call lock. It gives a shared pointer if the object is alive, or an empty one if it is gone. Inside the block, lock works and prints forty two. After the last owner dies, lock fails, and we print expired.

scenes.head: The three, side by side
scenes.say: Owners: one, many, or none. Copy: move only, adds an owner, adds an observer. Cost: as cheap as raw, a control block, shares that block.

scenes.head: The three, side by side (cont.)
scenes.say: Freed when: the owner dies, the last owner dies, never. Use: the default, truly shared, caches and cycles.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is R A I I? Resource acquisition is initialization. Constructor acquires, destructor releases. Why does it work? Destructors run on every exit: return, scope end, or exception. Examples? Unique pointer, lock guard, fstream.
rows: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor
destructors run on every exit, even a throw
cues: What is R A I I

scenes.say: Why smart pointers? They own and delete, so no leaks and no double frees. Which first? Unique pointer, as cheap as a raw pointer, move only. When shared? Only for truly shared ownership.
lines: They own and delete: no leaks, no double frees

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Unique, shared, weak? Unique: sole owner, move only. Shared: counted owners, freed with the last one. Weak: observes without owning. You lock it to use it.
rows: sole owner; move only; the default
counted owners; freed with the last

scenes.say: What is reference counting? Count the owners, and delete at zero. The rules? A copy adds one, a destroy subtracts one, a move changes nothing. Cost and trap? A control block, atomic updates, and cycles that never reach zero.
lines: control block, atomics; cycles never hit 0

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Circular reference problem? Two shared pointers own each other. Counts never reach zero. Symptom? No crash. Destructors never run, and memory leaks silently. Fix? Make one direction weak. Ownership should form a tree.
rows: A owns B, B owns A: counts never hit 0
no crash: destructors never run, a leak
weak back link; ownership is a tree

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these next. LeetCode two twenty six, invert binary tree: each node owned by its parent. LeetCode seven oh seven, design linked list: own and free every node. LeetCode one forty six, L R U cache: a list and a map.
rows: each node owned by its parent

scenes.say: So say this. R A I I: constructor acquires, destructor releases, even on a throw. Use unique pointer by default, and shared pointer only for shared ownership. Make back links weak, so ownership forms a tree.
lines: `weak_ptr` for back links: ownership is a tree.
